en: The Sūtra of the Ritual for the Accomplishment of the Bodhisattva Ārya-Krodhavajrakumāra,
Volume One, extracted from the Susiddhikara-mahāvidyārāja-tantra, Chapter Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of the Great Tang.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
withdrew to sit on one side, and joined his palms toward the Buddha.
And he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, World-Honored One, out of compassion you have sustained me.
You have already taught the ritual procedures, disciplinary codes, and instructional teachings for all *susiddhi* mantras."
I now desire, for the sake of sentient beings in the future and those lacking merit during the age of the Dharma’s decline—
who failed to cultivate wholesome qualities in previous lives and instead committed various sinful deeds— [to provide this teaching].
This leads to the retribution of poverty and destitution in this present life;
one encounters wicked people, engages in strife, litigation, and the killing of sentient beings,
and will likewise become a king in future lives.
While he ruled the kingdom according to the True Dharma and gave rise to pure faith, revering the Triple Gem,
the neighboring minor kings invaded his borders and did not follow the True Dharma; furthermore,
there were non-Buddhists who did not believe in cause and effect.
There are various such sentient beings who slander the Triple Gem and destroy the Buddha's teachings;
for their sake, [I now pray] before the Buddha.
He taught the methods for pacifying calamities, increasing prosperity, inspiring love and respect, and subjugating others,
thereby causing them to know that the Buddha-dharma possesses great majestic power and sovereign supernormal faculties,
and that all bodhisattvas are endowed with omniscience.
Furthermore, there may be those who cultivate the practices of mantra and conduct and see sentient beings who constantly harbor evil intentions,
seeking to destroy the Buddha-dharma by raising armies to harm the virtuous.
Out of great compassion and pity,
he performs the rite of subjugation so that those people shall not be pursued by their evil karma and are also shielded from falling into the evil realms in the future.
Therefore, this incomparable rite of the Greatly Majestic Holy Krodha-Karṇī is taught.
One who practices this rite should do so before a stūpa containing relics,
or by the bank of a river with clear, flowing water.
Whether in a secluded place, at a celestial shrine, or in the mountains—
in such locations as these—
he may sometimes drink milk and eat vegetables, or again, subsist on alms.
If one recites the mantra exclusively for six hundred thousand times,
then all previously practiced rites will achieve accomplishment and possess great efficacy;
one may even be able to bind and subdue various ghosts and demons.
Through the power of the mantra, it is possible to cause those who hold false views and slander the true Dharma,
as well as those who ruin the nation such as the icchantikas and their like, to all give rise to wholesome thoughts.
Poisonous insects and poisons cannot cause harm.
Furthermore, other practitioners of mantra-recitation from rival sects will be unable to subvert this dharma.
Even if a practitioner of mantra-recitation should fail to rely upon these ritual rules, [the protection remains].
Whether increasing or decreasing, it shall also be fulfilled;
furthermore, one can open all hidden treasures and break the bolts of the asuras.
It dries up rivers and causes flowing waters to turn back and cease.
Furthermore, first perform the ritual of taking one's own *rūdraka* fruit and mixing it with ox-gall and clarified butter.
He then lit a thousand lamps as an offering to the Holy Vajrakumāra,
whereupon a voice spoke from the air, saying, "Your dharma is now perfected."
One may then take arghya perfumed water and offer it upon one's forehead;
from this point forward, whatever one seeks shall be accomplished without exception.
Furthermore, one should proceed to the entrance of the asura cave.
Make a hook from *kuśa* grass.
Recite the mantra to empower the *kuśa* hook thoroughly,
and rotate it clockwise in the air beside the door.
Recite the mantra with single-minded devotion without interruption.
A great mass of fire will arise within the cave,
and all the asuras, both male and female, therein will be consumed by its flames.
Each of them manifested its own body and addressed the practitioner, saying:
"We pray that you, Venerable One, will enter our cave and sport therein as you please."
Having entered, he dwells there for one great eon, experiencing celestial delights.
Furthermore, if he wishes to retrieve a hidden treasure (nidhi), he need not choose a specific time or day;
he simply stands upon that treasure with one foot raised and recites the mantra.

Turning one's gaze clockwise to survey all four directions, one thereby establishes the boundary and constructs the great maṇḍala; this method is applied accordingly. Standing with focused mind and feet raised, one recites the mantra one hundred and eight times. If those who guard the hidden treasures should create obstacles or difficulties, [the practitioner shall subdue them].
It is immediately burned into a mass of fire.
The practitioner then says to them:
"Open this hidden treasure."
"Give me everything that is within your treasury.
If you do not give it, then speak thus:
'Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Maheśvara!'"
As well as the goddesses of battle, the nāgas,
and others who have come to suppress your hidden treasures;
you all should quickly give these things to me.
"If it be otherwise, the wrathful noble Vajrakumāra shall annihilate your family.
Having heard this, they all submitted in obedience and spoke to him as follows:
"You all may open the treasury yourselves and give it to me.
They then opened the treasury and respectfully brought it to him.
Furthermore, there is a method for taking realgar or orpiment as an *añjana* eye-salve.
Place it within a vessel of gold, silver,
or refined copper before a stūpa containing relics,
having smeared a square altar with incense.
Place an image of the noble Vajrakumāra in the center of the maṇḍala;
with various incenses, flowers, food offerings, and argha water,
invite him according to the instructions and make offerings to him.
Recite the mantra eight thousand times before this altar to consecrate the aforementioned medicine.
If signs of warmth appear,
apply it to the forehead or smear it into the eyes.
All who see it will feel drawn to it and give rise to joy in their hearts.
If the sign of smoke appears,
by employing it as before, one will immediately attain the accomplishment of *āṭanāṭa*.
If a light-sign appears,
one likewise attains mastery in soaring through the air as described previously.
Furthermore, there is a method for reaching the Ganges or a river that flows into the ocean.
One who performs the recitation by this riverbank, whether eating pure food or fasting,
shall recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and reach the cave of the asuras.
Forming mudrās and reciting mantras,
the bolts of the asuras were spontaneously shattered and the cave gates opened;
the asura king then led [the practitioner] into the palace.
By consuming the celestial nectar (*amṛta*), one’s lifespan shall last for one kalpa.

Furthermore, according to the ritual method, if one forms the mudrā and recites the mantra while facing the waters of the great ocean at the shore of the vast sea, [the desired result will be attained].
The water immediately receded by twenty-five cubits;
wherever it receded, the ground became parched dry.
Furthermore, he closed his eyes at the edge of the seashore.
Block both ears with cotton,
form the mudrā, and recite the mantra one thousand times;
then one will see oneself arrive at the summit of Mount Laṅkā.

Furthermore, if one recites it one thousand times, the rākṣasa king Vibiṣaṇa will manifest in a majestic and handsome form and come to serve as a servant to the reciter; if he does not submit to being employed,
[the practitioner shall compel him].
One should then imagine that the rākṣasa is beneath one’s left foot; as the foot is lifted and pressed against the ground,
the rākṣasa king faints and dies,
and the city of Laṅkā where he dwells is entirely consumed by fire like a great mass of flames.
The practitioner of recitation should give rise to a mind of compassion.
By adding the syllable *svāhā* to the mantra phrases,
those rākṣasas and others will immediately recover their breath, submit, and become available for one's command.
Furthermore, before the deity Kumārarāja,
one should ride upon the peacock deity and, while fasting,
recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.
The deity shall manifest its form and grant the practitioner's wishes.
The practitioner then takes the arghya water, consecrates it seven times with mantras,
and offers it.
He spoke, saying, "Welcome, Kumāra!
I pray that I may attain accomplishment in all the mantras taught by the god Kumāra Maheśvara."
He said, "May you achieve success," and having spoken,
he vanished. From that time forward,
throughout all the Vajra families, [this was established].
Furthermore, all mantras spoken by other devas shall be accomplished.
Moreover, according to another method, one should not eat upon reaching the temple of Maheśvara and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
All that the mind desires and seeks shall be fully satisfied.
Furthermore, [one will receive offerings] from Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, Maheśvara, Śakra Devendra, Kumāra, Sūrya, and all other such deities.
If one recites the mantra one hundred thousand times before an image, whatever wishes the mind seeks shall all be accomplished.
Furthermore, if one desires to subjugate wicked people,
one should take mustard seeds mixed with salt and perform a homa sacrifice.
Recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
for each recitation, utter the person's name once and cast it into the fire.
Even devas and asuras will be destroyed.
How much more so for other human beings who harbor malicious intentions—it would not harm them.
Even for one who has no prior merit or accomplishments, success follows with every recitation; how much more so for one who constantly upholds it.
Furthermore, if one wishes to transform a *milidaka* into gold and jewels,
one should take a *milidaka* and step upon its head with the left foot.
Strike it with the hand seal;
with the mantra including the syllable HŪṂ,
that Mahādeva shall arise of his own accord.
One strikes it with a sword made of *puṣpa-āyasa* iron, whereupon the entire body immediately transforms into gold.
If this does not occur, the reciter shall say: "Quickly eject! Quickly eject!"
He immediately spat out a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), which he suspended beneath his neck; whatever he desired was thereby fully accomplished.
Furthermore, there is a method [to perform this] before a stūpa containing relics (śarīra).
Recite the mantra six hundred thousand times;
thus, the preliminary practice will be accomplished.
Then, fashion a sword from *puṣpa* iron.
Measure the length as six, eight, sixteen, or twelve finger-widths.
Wash it with the five pure substances.
Holding the sword in the right hand within the *maṇḍala*, perform the recitation.
Until the sword manifests blazing flames,
one attains the power to transform the body into that of a Vidyādhara and fly through the void;
this is called the Sword-Wielding Vidyādhara.
Alternatively, one may fashion a vajra from *puṣpa* iron,
with dimensions as described in the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
The recitation is performed as before.
Then he transforms into the Lord of the Vināyakas,
a ṛṣi who has attained mastery over all hosts of māras; or,
by performing the wheel-recitation as before, he becomes the Cakravartin ṛṣi.
One becomes a sovereign among the vidyādharas;
if one performs the recitation with the battle-axe as before, one becomes a sovereign among the yakṣas and a master of the vidyādharas.
One attains mastery over all the yakṣas.
If one fashions a knife, one becomes a ṛṣi who is the mistress of the goddesses of the heavens and attains mastery over all celestial nymphs;
if one fashions a lasso, one becomes a ṛṣi who is the lord of the nāgas.
One attains mastery over all nāgas;
if one performs the *śakti* rite, one gains courageous strength and great power,
capable of rivaling the god Kumāra.
If one performs the *khaṭvāṅga*, one will become like the god Maheśvara,
attaining sovereignty over the three realms with respect to all aforementioned dharmas.
If one accomplishes this single dharma, one will be able to enter all maṇḍalas and also accomplish all dharmas.
One will come and go together with all the vidyādharas and have a lifespan of one great kalpa.
Furthermore, before the entrance to the Asura cave where one has previously entered,
recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
This applies to one who has first achieved mastery through recitation within that cave.
Go out to meet him, prostrate, and lead him into the palace.
If he descends, go immediately to the temple of Maheśvara and recite the mantra one thousand times while uttering the syllable *HŪṂ*.
Those who had previously entered the palace all came forth.
Furthermore, there is a method for taking the withered flowers offered to Maheśvara,
and also taking a painted image of Maheśvara.
Standing with his left foot upon her head,
he performs a homa offering using withered flowers;
thus, Śrīdevī and the asura women [will appear].
Emerging from the cave, he came before the practitioner and spoke these words:
"I shall serve the Venerable One for the rest of my life."
The practitioner claps his hands three times and declares:
"Follow me! The master then arouses a mind of compassion within the phrases of the mantra.

They will all awaken.
If, by performing this rite, they still do not enter, [then...]
Then, closing one's eyes, one recites the mantra.
Thereupon, Vajrakumāra manifests his form and addresses the practitioner, saying:
"Come, enter; you and your retinue may also enter."
Furthermore, if one wishes to summon a rākṣasa messenger,
one must first enter the maṇḍala and receive empowerment;
in this way, one will be free from fear.
Constantly contemplate all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas;
perform repentance, sympathetic joy, entreaty, dedication, and aspiration during the three periods of the day.
Then, place the image within a cemetery and construct a fierce and powerful maṇḍala.
Wearing red garments and adorning one's body with garlands of red flowers,
with a human *kapāla* placed upon the head,
one should recite the mantra without limit.
Constantly donning armor upon one’s body, one should draw a maṇḍala of four seals within a fierce and sharp ritual arena.
At the time of the initial recitation, one sees a dog of evil form with its fangs protruding upward.
Some have hideous forms with upright garlands;
some have one foot, three feet, or eight arms;
some have two heads or four heads.
Alternatively, one may see great winds, thunder, and rain.
During the second week, one sees a beautiful woman with a finely adorned body who appears illusory and seductive;
by giving rise to the contemplation of loving-kindness, she recedes and no longer appears.
On the third seven-day period, he saw the Vināyakas and Rākṣasas of extremely fierce appearance;
he immediately subdued them and made them his messengers.
If one sees another accomplished vidyādhara who has attained siddhi and gives rise to even a slight wrathful gaze toward that person,
all of that person's accomplishments and dharmas will completely fall away.
Those rākṣasas and others made a vow:
"In whatever we are commanded to do or wherever we are sent,
we shall carry out all tasks and serve as messengers."
Furthermore, there is another method: in an old garden, or beneath a single tree,
or by the side of a pond, or in a mountain valley— whichever place one finds pleasing—
one should remain silent.
Whether begging for food, drinking milk,
eating vegetables, or sustaining one's life by any means,
if one performs repentance at the three times of day and recites the mantra eight hundred thousand times before an image, all that one intends to do will be accomplished.
Furthermore, if one wishes to stop an enemy so that they cannot cause harm,
one should abstain from food for three days and draw a maṇḍala of four seals,
making offerings accordingly.
At the position of the Bodhisattva Ekajaṭī within the maṇḍala,
place a green banner atop a bamboo pole.

Mix sword-dust with clay to fashion the shape of a single-pronged vajra,
and construct a homa fire pit.
Within the furnace, he further molds a small, single-pronged vajra.
He kindles a fire with thorny wood and takes bone powder mixed with poison.
Recite the mantra once and utter their name once,
casting [the substance] into the hearth while performing the rite before the military array;
this shall cause the entire host to become blind and the weapons in their hands to fall away of their own accord.
Alternatively, one remains motionless at that spot like a tree stump.
Furthermore, when the enemy army intends to press close,
one allows them to draw near for a time.
Having recently established the four-seal mandala as previously described,
other mandalas may also be used.
Erect the aforementioned blue banner directly opposite the front of the enemy army.
Construct the homa hearth.
The practitioner, naked and with hair disheveled,
forms mudrās and dons armor to protect the body.
Take the Mahāmāṃsava poison and blood;
recite the mantra one hundred and eight times at each of the three periods of the day,
calling out the person's name and casting [the substances] into the fire.
Within seven days, they will kill one another and incite one another to murder until all have perished;
within two weeks, they will be utterly extinguished without remainder.
While reciting the mantra, one must not speak.
When sleeping and resting, one should lie upon a cowhide.
Furthermore, there is a method wherein one draws blood from the five pulse-points on the crown of one's own head and performs homa with it.
If his enemies are for a moment stubborn and deluded like a tree stump, they may be seized and slain at will;
yet if they submit in accordance with the Dharma, he immediately gives rise to a mind of compassion and takes ghee mixed with honey.
Forming the name of the person in question with *nāgakeśara* pollen, recite the mantra once for each casting into the fire; their sufferings will all be pacified.
Regarding the aforementioned methods:
If one dharma is accomplished,
then one will be able to accomplish entry into all maṇḍalas as well.
All the vidyā-siddhas of all dharmas shall come and go with him for the duration of one great kalpa.
Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, will provide protection for him.
Take seven earthworm castings and fashion them into the form of that deity;
then, with the right foot, step upon its heart.
Take poison mixed with rudrākṣa and white mustard seeds.
Recite the mantra one thousand times.
For each recitation, cast one oblation into the fire.
Thus, you will gain the veneration and love of Śakra, and his celestial retinue will constantly come to protect you.
Furthermore, if one empowers a flower or fruit by reciting this mantra seven times and gives it to someone, that person will become joyful.
This Vajrakumāra mantra should be recited before a stūpa containing śarīra.
In other places, one should not perform recitation, as the ritual procedures will not be accomplished.
However, if one constantly recites without interruption,
all that is sought shall be achieved.
One should generate the bodhicitta and abandon thoughts of stinginess;
one should distance oneself from useless worldly talk,
so that all supreme vows may manifest before one.
One must not allow oneself to be taken advantage of by various māras.
One should not treat human illnesses or cure demonic possessions,
as this would obstruct the Great Dharma.
Regarding the sequence of the mantra, mudrā, and recitation: for the root mudrā, join the two middle fingers back-to-back and extend them upward;
cross the two ring fingers horizontally across the outer side of the middle joints of the middle fingers.
Hook the tips of the two index fingers with the tips of the two ring fingers.
The two thumbs should touch at the tips of the middle joints in front of the middle fingers.
The tips of the two little fingers should be joined together and held upright, pointing downward like needles.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo ratnatrayāya | Namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye | Mahāyakṣasenāpate | Tadyathā | Oṃ | Kaṇidūni | Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā || Furthermore, this is the second root mantra.
To open the palace of the asuras, use the aforementioned root mudrā.
The mantra is as follows: *Namo ratnatrayāya | namo vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpate | tadyathā | oṃ dūna vidūna kaṇi kuruḍa sarvāntarani hūṃ*. Next, bind the single-pronged vajra mudrā.
Interlace the two hands within to form fists;
cross the two thumbs over the backs of the two little fingers.
With the index fingers held upright and joined at the tips of the nails, employ the first root mantra mentioned previously.
Next, bind the protection-of-the-body mudrā.
Use the previously mentioned root mudrā to seal the five places of the body.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ sarvanuṣṭhāvakarakaṇigurudharakṣaṃ svāhā. (4) Next, perform the armor-binding mudrā (*kavaca-mudrā*).
Following the previous root mudrā,
extend the two index fingers so that they touch at their tips,
and with the two thumbs, pinch the first joint beneath the two index fingers.
Seal the five places of the body.
The mantra is:
Oṃ hṛīḥ karṇaye manohe huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Third, bind the Jewel Mountain Seal.
Following the previous mudrā of the pestle,
slightly bend the tips of the two index fingers so that their heads touch;
placing it upon the head completes the rite.
The mantra is:
Oṃ ājara hūṃ. Second, perform the mudrā for binding the walls and boundaries, following the previous root mudrā.
Straighten both index fingers with their tips about one inch apart. The mantra is:
Oṃ hṛīḥ kaṇe naha naha paca paca hūṃ phaṭ. Next, form the *jāla-mudrā* (net seal).
Following the previous root mudrā,
extend the two index fingers outward and separate them.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajrapañjara hūṃ phaṭ. Second, perform the seal of the Vināyakas, following the previous root seal.
Bend the two index fingers and the two middle fingers into the palms.
Place each of the two thumbs over the respective middle fingers within the palms, extending them so they face away from each other, and join them to form a fist.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ viduṣa viduṣatrasāya śūṣāya sarvavidyādhināthāya hūṃ svāhā. Next, form the mudrā for inviting the noble one.
Following the previous fundamental procedure,
beckon toward oneself with the two index fingers.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ dundini phaṭ. (2) Second, to bind and invite the assembly of the Noble One’s retinue, use the previous mudrā and recite the mantra:
Oṃ saparivāra-māvāhaya āgaccha kani-kuru samayam anusmara svāhā. (5) Fifth, to bind the offering of arghya, use the mudrā.
Following the root mudrā, join the two thumbs to press against the first joints of the two index fingers. The mantra is:
Oṃ vajranāga hūṃ. Second, perform the seat-offering mudrā.
Perform the seal of the single-pronged vajra as before;
join the two thumbs to press against the lower joints of the two index fingers, with the tips extending slightly outward. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajravīraya svāhā. Third, perform the mudrā for offering scented unguent;
it is the same as the previous mudrā of the vajra.
Slightly bend both thumbs and press them against the lower part of the index fingers;
the two thumbs should be separated by approximately two inches.
This will fulfill any deficiencies in the ritual procedures.
The mantra is:
Oṃ kaṇi-kuru-dha sarva-sattva-sakara rakṣa sarva-sandhāni svāhā. Fourth, perform the mudrā for offering flowers.
Following the previous method, for the mūdrā of the pestle, extend the right index finger;
the mantra is: Oṃ kaṇipūṣpa-munāpava hūṃ. Second, form the seal of incense.
As before, join the two thumbs face-to-face in the mudrā of the pestle. The mantra is:
Oṃ kaṇi-kuru-dha ugra-ṇeṣṭaru dṛkṭa-paira-vāsara-hana hana dhuṃ phaṭ svāhā. Fifth, perform the mudrā for offering food.
Following the previous mudrā of the pestle, extend the tips of the two thumbs and the two little fingers so that they touch one another.
Interlace the remaining six fingers inwardly to form a fist. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ kaṇi hūṃ hūṃ svāhā. Fourth, perform the lamp-light mudrā. It is modeled after the previous vajra mudrā;
extend the two index fingers toward the body and join them upright. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ kaṇi ṇi pi pi pāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Fourth, the head-binding mudrā.
Following the previous root mudrā, with the two thumbs pressing upon the nails of the two ring fingers, recite the mantra:
Oṃ hūṃ mama phaṭ. Third, form the crown mudrā.
Following the previous root mudrā, extend both index fingers straight with their tips touching. The mantra is:
Oṃ hṛīḥ caṇḍakani naha paca hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Next, bind the aforementioned root mudrā and place it upon the heart.
To empower with the heart-mantra, the heart-mantra is:
Oṃ kaṇi hūṃ phaṭ. Second, bind the armor mudrā as the mudrā of Tārā Bodhisattva.
Slightly open the two hands.
Recite the aforementioned Armor Mantra,
and then form the Supreme Mudrā.
Interlace the two hands within to form fists;
join the tips of the two little fingers together.
Employ the aforementioned second root mantra.
Next, hold the rosary at the heart and empower it seven times with the *Cittamantra* (Heart Mantra).
The *Cittamantra* is as follows:
Oṃ kāniduma hūṃ phaṭ. Fourth, perform the seal for sending off the Noble One (*ārya*).
Following the previous root seal, extend the two index fingers outward and recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ kaṇi svāhā. Now, furthermore, the mudrā for opening the door to the asura cave is taught.
The practitioner should swiftly step upon the ground.

he knits his brows and puffs out both cheeks;
he raises both hands high, curling the ten fingers to form the claws of a lion.

from time to time, with his two hands acting as the two claws of a lion,
he alternately treads upon the ground while walking in the manner of a lion.
Perform the dance of the *ariṣṭa* while circumambulating.
Visualize yourself as the deity.

take an uncut piece of white cotton cloth.

adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.
His body is the color of fire,
with flames streaming forth from his entire form;
he holds a vajra in his right hand.
The sword is raised upward;
the left hand forms the mudrā of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*);
the feet are in the *līlā-sthānaka* posture, standing upon a flat rock.
The hand is in the boon-granting (varada) gesture. Below, depict the practitioner,
kneeling with the right knee on the ground and holding an incense burner in his hand.
Once the image has been completed,
one should perform various kinds of offerings before it, burning安息香 (an-xi-xiang,
*agaru* or *alambuṣa*) incense while reciting the mantra without interruption.
Furthermore, one hears voices from the air and the sound of bells;
again, light appears like a shooting star,
falling into the center of the maṇḍala with a sound like a thunderclap.
Immediately offer argha water.
If the image moves or emits light, one should know that it has produced an efficacious result;
thereafter, when reciting mantras before the image, all will be accomplished according to one's wishes.

This image depicts the Buddha alone, emerging from the ocean.
His body is the color of vaidūrya and has six arms;
his upper and lower limbs are well-proportioned and his physical features are full and complete.
His face has three eyes, and these eyes are red in color.
He wears a jeweled crown with canine fangs protruding upward;
his mouth bites his lower lip, and his brows are knit in a fierce and wrathful expression.
Furthermore, within the ocean, paint a single mountain of jewels.
The image stands with its left foot treading upon a jewel mountain,
atop which a wondrous lotus flower supports that foot;
the right foot stands in the waters of the ocean, submerged up to the mid-knee.
In his right hand, he holds a *ṭiḷiśaṅkha* vajra,
making a straightening gesture;
in his second hand, he holds a *musala* club.
That is to say, one end of the staff is shaped like an iron pestle;
the third hand holds a battle-axe,
and the first left hand grasps the staff.
The second hand is in the gesture of poised readiness;
it forms a vajra-fist with the index finger extended.
The third hand holds a sword.
He bound large snakes upon his body as shoulder-straps;
furthermore, he wore all manner of venomous snakes as bracelets,
armlets, waist-bands, necklaces, and earrings, and used them to bind his hair.
Furthermore, a great serpent encircles his waist three times;
his back is surrounded by a circular halo of flaming fire,
and outside the flames there are clouds and lightning.
Having assisted one another in this way,
once the painting is finished, one should carry it to a riverbank, or toward the foot of a tree,
or into a temple, or to the side of a pond.
When reciting the mantra, one must always beg for food and remain silent,
not speaking with others; furthermore,
until the accomplishment is achieved, one must constantly maintain a mind of loving-kindness.
One should confess and repent during the three periods of the day;
one must diligently exhort oneself to generate a courageous mind and not be timid,
always delighting in renunciation and giving.
Each month, one should receive empowerment and perform the protection of the body.
At the site of recitation, one should bind the boundaries of the cardinal directions and the boundary of the maṇḍala.
Having empowered scented water, one should sprinkle it upon oneself, one’s clothing, and one’s garments.
Three times each day, invite the Noble One,
offer argha water, unguents, food, and lamps,
and recite the mantra nine hundred thousand times before the image.
Perform the preliminary rites.
While reciting the mantra correctly, if any evil person comes to create obstacles or difficulties,
gaze at them while reciting the mantra with wrath.
That person will immediately become epileptic and deranged.
If one recites [the mantra] while looking at them while calling their name,
their body flesh will split apart piece by piece.
Or, if one has reached the point of death and no worldly physician can save them,
they should for a moment press down firmly on the ground with the big toe of their right foot while reciting the mantra.
Then fire will rain down from the sky, burning him fiercely.
If he arouses a mind of compassion and recites the mantra,
it will be as water extinguishing fire, and he shall immediately attain awakening.
If external enemies invade the borders,
when the commander-in-chief recites this mantra,
that army will all be stricken with pestilence.
Some may flee in panic,
some may wither and die, or suffer from the affliction of epilepsy;
yet if they submit and comply, through compassionate recitation, they shall return to their former state.
Furthermore, for one who seeks to achieve a sublime result,
during the bright fortnight of a month of supernatural powers,
one should go to the shore of a sea or a river and fashion stupas by imprinting patterns in the sand or the mud.
Place the Verse on Dependent Origination—the Verse of the Dharma-body Relic—in the center; place the image before the stūpa.
The practitioner of recitation shall eat parched grain mixed with water.
Take *arka* wood and dip it in clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
After performing one hundred thousand fire-offering *homa* oblations,
the earth will shake and the practitioner’s body will fly upward to become the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
If torches appear throughout the entire land, [the same result shall follow].
One then becomes a lord of the Four Heavenly Kings.
It is as if great clouds pour down rain upon the great earth, causing all hidden treasures to emerge simultaneously,
or as if golden light appears everywhere.
Then that bodhisattva’s lifespan shall be one kalpa;
possessing great majestic power, they cannot be thwarted or destroyed.
If they see all sentient beings’ bodies emitting flames of light, [they perceive them as such].
One will immediately realize and awaken to all the Buddha-dharma of the three vehicles.
Bodhicitta will be accomplished,
and images and stūpas will emit light.
Then one will become a king among all the vidyādhara sages.
If light-flames radiate throughout the ten directions,
one will see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
All supreme aspirations, whether worldly or supramundane, that one seeks shall be fully satisfied.
This Dharma should not be entrusted to those who lack wisdom, who have little compassion,
or who do not respect their teachers and elders and are prone to verbal transgressions.
For those who are restless and distracted, who have many worldly affairs,
who have not entered a maṇḍala, and who have not received initiation—
such persons may perform recitation.
This will bring about madness, untimely death, and a shortened lifespan;
thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
Furthermore, if a neighboring country invades the borders or wicked ministers incite rebellion, [the following shall be performed].
Taking the hair of the person against whom one has a grievance,
grind it into powder and knead it into the shape of that person. Then,
at a cemetery or by the side of a pond, [perform the rite].
With the image facing north and the practitioner facing south,
place the image within a triangular mandala.
Cease speech, beg for alms, and adopt a wrathful state of mind devoid of compassion.
Form a vajra-fist with the right hand,
extend the little finger, and pierce the heart of the person's form;
recite the mantra without interruption.
By this power, he causes that person to suffer a great illness;
then, within the mandala, the Wrathful King manifests his body,
appearing like the size of a thumb joint.
Like a mass of fire with the color of molten gold,
it flows out in a circle as vajra flames;
with the index finger of the right hand, one makes the gesture of threatening.
He immediately went swiftly to that place and declared:
"A certain practitioner has sent me here to take your life."
"Your life shall not be preserved.
Upon hearing these words, he immediately spat out warm blood and his life ended.
Had he submitted and repented, [he would have lived].
One should arouse a mind of loving-kindness and quickly empower scented water to sprinkle upon their heads;
they will then be freed from suffering and distress and regain their composure.
If one sees other accomplished practitioners who have attained *siddhi*, [one should likewise act].
If one gives rise to even a slight anger toward that person, all of their accomplished dharmas will completely perish.
Furthermore, regarding the method for driving away evil persons and making them depart to a distance:
Take *laṅgali* medicine and recite the mantra while calling the person's name seven times;
bury it beneath the threshold of that person's door, and they will depart of their own accord.
Furthermore, there is another method: fashion an image of Vajrakumāra from white sandalwood measuring three finger-widths in height,
holding a single-pronged vajra in his right hand.
The left hand is in the mudrā of granting boons;
he has a wrathful form with his lower lip bitten;
and he is adorned with ornaments in the shape of vajras.
Make a casket from *vibhītaka* wood and place it therein;
burn *sugandha* incense as an offering and recite the mantra thirty thousand times before the casket.
One will immediately achieve a thousandfold increase in both stature and size.
There is no need to select specific days or times, nor is there any requirement for fasting or ritual observances;
even those who have not achieved success before may attain it.
If a person encounters calamity or distress, by reciting the name of that [deity], they shall attain liberation.
Furthermore, one should subsist on vegetables, drink milk, or beg for food while reciting;
one should observe the prohibitive precepts exactly as a bhikṣu does.
Recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times for whatever purpose or task one intends.
Before this image, perform the binding and prostration as previously described;
all that is asked shall be granted with manifest efficacy.
Furthermore, regarding the method for realgar: as before, one should paint an image.
Take realgar and place it in a vessel of refined copper.
The practitioner should take the five pure substances and drink them.
The body shall immediately become pure.
Place the image before the śarīra-stūpa and purify the vihāra using the root mantra.
Having bound the protection of the body and the boundaries of the cardinal and intermediate directions,
one should perform offerings by consecrating the unguents, incense, seasonal flowers, food, and lamps with the previously mentioned mantra of the retinue.
Alternatively, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should use four-cornered bodhi leaves to support a vessel containing realgar,
and cover it with three bodhi leaves.
Alternatively, one may also use leaves from the *bodhivṛkṣa* tree.
One should perform the recitation until the three signs appear;
if the sign of "warmth" appears, take some of it and smear it on one's feet.
Immediately, rising one chi above the ground, he travels a thousand li daily.
If the sign of smoke appears, he attains *āntardhāna* (invisibility).
If the sign of light appears, he soars into the void.
Nothing whatsoever can obstruct or destroy it.
If one encounters elephants, horses, or carriages on the road, they will spontaneously clear a path to avoid him.
When the practitioner performs the rite, [this occurs].
One should wear yellow robes and a yellow *śikhā-sūtra* (sacred thread) draped over the shoulder like a *kāṣāya*.
If seeking the accomplishment of *āñjana*,
one should dye the clothing with blue clay and wear it.
Alternatively, one may wear red garments; the ritual for the divine thread is likewise.
It is taught that the maṇḍala should be constructed during the dark fortnight of either the fifth or ninth month.
First, one must cause the practitioner to reverently make offerings to the master.
Then, take auspicious wood twelve finger-widths long;
empower it one thousand and eight times,
and perform homa for the sake of the practitioner who intends to recite the mantra.
When about to lead [the disciple] into the maṇḍala for the conferral of empowerment,
one who has previously performed the preparatory rites (pūrvasevā) should draw the maṇḍala.
Using five-colored powders, form four gates;
outside the gates, draw boundary markers.
Divide the maṇḍala into three sections.
Taking half of the central portion, it serves as the gateway;
above the gateway, one should draw the Buddha seated upon a lotus with fragrant powder,
and to the right, draw the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
On the left, depict the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
seated together upon a lotus;
below the entrance, depict the noble wrathful Vajrakumāra Cāṇḍa.
He stands upon a lotus, his entire body ablaze with light.
At each of the four corners, one should draw a three-pronged vajra entwined by snakes and emitting flames.
At each gate, place an auspicious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*).
At the center of the altar, place one vase,
filled with scented water and its neck tied with fine silk cloth.
Each [mantra] is empowered one hundred and eight times.
Filled with vajra-water, it is used to sprinkle upon the crown of the disciple’s head.
Once sprinkled, all siddhis shall manifest before them.
From this point onward, as soon as one forms the mudrā and performs the recitation,
immeasurable merit will be instantaneously accumulated,
and all that is sought shall be accomplished.
